messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 29
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Combat Pilot
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 60

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Discomfort: Feeling uncomfortable, Event Recall: Talking about the event, Loss Themes: Talk about people loosing loved ones
  Maladaptive Strategies: Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma, Avoid Reminders: Being reminded of the event by others, Avoid New Relationships: Starting new friendships or relationships
  Memory: Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over., Photographic Recall: Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind., Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
  Negative Appraisals: Defective Self: There is something wrong with me as a person, Can't Rely on Others: I can't rely on other people, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed

Vignette:
Anika had always prided herself on her control, a necessary trait for a combat pilot. It was a quality she cultivated in the cockpit and in her life. But for the last eight months, since the accident, that control had been an illusion. The event itself was a blur of screeching tires and shattering glass on a rain-slicked highway. She had been driving her younger brother home from a weekend visit. One moment they were laughing, the next there was the sickening lurch of impact. The memory of it didn’t come to her as a coherent story, but as a series of disjointed, high-definition snapshots: the spiderweb crack in the windshield, the precise look of shock on her brother’s face, the dashboard crumpled against his legs. Sometimes, these images would flash in her mind’s eye with the clarity of photographs she was being forced to look at. Other times, the entire sequence would unspool against her will, a relentless film playing over and over, always ending in the same deafening silence before the sirens began.

In the weeks that followed, Anika returned to duty, believing the familiar rigor of her job would be a shield. Instead, it became a minefield. During a pre-flight check, the familiar, snug click of her harness locking into place sent a jolt through her. Suddenly, she wasn’t in her F-16 anymore; she was pinned in the driver’s seat, the seatbelt digging into her collarbone, overwhelmed by a physical sense of discomfort so profound it left her breathless. This became a pattern: an innocuous trigger in her surroundings would, without warning, bring the full memory rushing back. She started trying to fight it, to push the thoughts away with brute force. When the film started to play, she would stare at the rivets on the cockpit canopy, counting them one by one, a desperate attempt to anchor herself in the present and silence the past.

Socially, she began constructing walls. The well-meaning condolences from friends and colleagues felt hollow. Phrases like “He’s in a better place” only reinforced a growing conviction that she couldn't rely on other people to understand a pain this deep. When her parents called, their attempts to talk about her brother, to share a happy memory, felt like prodding a raw wound. She would find an excuse to end the call, certain that engaging with the topic would only make the images in her head more vivid. At the squadron, when a fellow pilot casually mentioned losing an uncle years ago, Anika felt a surge of panic and had to physically leave the briefing room. She began to actively steer clear of any conversation that touched on loss. When a new officer joined her unit and tried to strike up a friendship, Anika kept her replies short and her posture closed. The thought of starting a new relationship, of letting someone in, was terrifying. She had come to believe there was something fundamentally wrong with her, that she was broken in a way no one else was. The central, haunting appraisal that echoed in her quietest moments was that she should have protected him. She was the older sister, the pilot, the one who was supposed to be in control. She had failed in that single, critical duty.

Her isolation deepened. The avoidance that was meant to protect her was now costing her the very connections she needed. It was her commanding officer who finally intervened, noting her withdrawal and a subtle hesitation in her movements that hadn't been there before. He mandated the clinical evaluation. Anika now sits in the therapist’s office, not out of a belief that she can be fixed, but out of professional obligation. What she wants, more than anything, is for the film to stop playing. She is terrified that it never will, that she will be trapped forever with those photographic stills of the worst moment of her life, forever the sister who failed to protect her brother.
